parts: You have been walking since dawn. The path left the forest behind, then the hills, then everything that still looked like a country, and now it leads nowhere but to the tower.

The tower rises before you. However far back you tilt your head, you cannot see the top: it goes into the clouds, and the clouds do not give it back. Its stones are grey and worn, covered in moss up to the height of a man. Higher up, windows. Higher still, more windows, smaller and smaller, until your eyes give up.

They say no one has ever reached the top. They also say that at the top there is a door, and that behind that door there is something everyone is looking for without being able to name it. You have come to see.

Three ways lie open to you. The great wooden door, ajar, with a thread of yellow light slipping out. An old dry well at the foot of the wall, its rim warm to the touch. And the ivy, thick as an arm, climbing as far as your eye can follow.
If you go through the great door, turn to {}.
If you climb down the well, turn to {}.
If you climb the ivy, turn to {}.
You jump onto the big wheel, and it welcomes you without a shudder. It is so wide that you can sit on it, between two teeth, as on a step. And it rises.

It rises slowly, so slowly that you have time to look around. The other wheels, below, bustle like insects. The pendulums swing to and fro. You can make out, far below, the workshop and its dusty window.
The wheel carries you, slow and sure, up to the ceiling, where a round trapdoor opens. You slip through it, and you come out into the open air.

The wind slaps your face. You are outside, on the side of the tower, above the void, on a narrow stone ledge. And before you, immense, is the face of the clock. Its numerals are taller than you. Its two hands of black iron, as long as ships' masts, point upwards, almost one on top of the other. It will soon be noon. Or midnight.
If you look at the time, turn to {}.
If you grab the minute hand to climb higher, turn to {}.
You have not eaten since dawn. You lift the ladle with both hands, dip it, and blow on it.
The soup is delicious. Truly delicious: thick, fragrant, with that spicy taste you still cannot place, which warms you down to your toes. You have some more. Then a little more.
Behind you, heavy footsteps make the saucepans rattle on their hooks. A door opens. A deep voice hums a song without words.
You turn round. The cook is back. She is very wide and very tall, she carries a basket of turnips under each arm, and her front teeth, long and yellow, stick out over her lip. She is an ogress.
She has not seen you yet. She puts down her baskets. She looks for her apron.
If you pay her a compliment, turn to {}.
If you keep the ladle to defend yourself, turn to {}.
You pull the rope. Once, gently, then harder.
The bell swings. The clapper strikes the bronze.

The sound that comes out is not a sound. It is a wall. It hits you from everywhere at once, it goes through you, it shakes your ribs and your teeth and the inside of your skull. The ledge vibrates under your feet. The clock face vibrates. The whole tower vibrates like a violin string.
You are right underneath. You had not thought of that.

Then nothing. An immense silence, total, woolly. You see the bell still swinging, the clapper striking again, but you no longer hear it. You no longer hear anything. Not the wind, not your heart, not your own voice when you shout.
Nor do you hear it when your feet slip off the ledge. You do not even hear yourself fall.

The painter puts down his brush. He stays silent for a moment, looking at his canvas, which shows a floor of the tower half finished: arches, a window, a bit of staircase that does not lead anywhere yet.
"The top," he says at last. "I haven't painted it yet."

He explains that he has tried, of course. Several times. But every time he reaches the top of the canvas, something is missing. A detail. A colour. He does not know what. So he adds another floor while he waits to find it, and the tower grows, and the top moves further away.
"The sphinx, up above, knows what is missing," he says. "She knows a great many things. But she does not give them away, she makes you look for them."

He shows you, at the back of the studio, a small wooden ladder leading up to a trapdoor. "That way. Be careful with her questions. And if you find out what is missing, come back and tell me. It would help me along."
Climb up to the sphinx, and turn to {}.
You take your time. You let a long silence pass, as the gardener advised, or as your caution whispers to you. Then you answer:
The sphinx closes her eyes. A slow smile comes to her lips, without teeth, this time.
"Age, yes," she says. "It always goes up. It never comes down. Even here, where time has stopped at one minute to noon, it goes up." She opens her eyes again. "Would you like to know mine?"
She does not wait for your answer. She stretches out a claw, and on the marble step in front of you she traces a number, deep in the stone, as if in butter:
"Thirty-two centuries," she says. "That is a long time to wait for the right answer. Keep it. You will need it higher up, with the other two. And tell no one: it is very rude to reveal a lady's age."
Then she rises, slowly, and steps aside to let you pass.
Climb the staircase, and turn to {}.

You hook your lantern to your belt and start climbing. The shaft is so narrow that you can wedge your back against one wall and your feet against the other. You climb like that, in little pushes, for what feels like hours.

The rock turns to brick. The brick turns black, greasy, covered in soot. You realise that you are no longer in a chimney of the mountain, but in a chimney of the tower, a real one, the kind used for making fires. Fortunately, the fire is out. Has been for a long time, judging by the colour of the ashes.
At last, light. You let yourself slide, you land on a heap of cold ashes in a cloud of dust, and you sit in the hearth for a moment, coughing.
Before you stretches a large, silent room. You see shelves. A great many shelves.
Climb out of the hearth, and turn to {}.

You reach the foot of a broad and majestic staircase, with steps of yellow marble, rising between two columns towards a golden light. It is hot here, as in a desert. It smells of sand, incense, and wild beast.
On the steps, stretched out at full length, lies a sphinx.

Immense. The body of a lion, with powerful muscles under sand-coloured fur, wings folded on the back, and the face of a woman, very beautiful, very ancient, very calm, with eyes slit like a cat's. They say "the sphinx", but she is a lady, and a very old one. Her tail beats slowly on the marble. Her claws are out, laid in front of her like knives on a tablecloth.
She is not asleep. She has been watching you come from the start, without a flicker of her eyelashes.
Around her, on the steps, there are things you would rather not look at too closely. Belt buckles. Boots. A lantern, like yours.
She blocks the whole staircase. To get past, you have to get past her.
If you approach her, turn to {}.
If you attack her, turn to {}.
"A way out?" The painter raises his eyebrows, then smiles. "Why not. Nobody ever asks me for one."

He takes a fresh canvas, sets it on the easel, and paints. Quickly, with astonishing talent. A door, open. And behind the door, a meadow in the sun, with a path heading off towards some hills. You recognise the path: it is the one you came by, before the tower.
"There you are," he says. "Off you go."
You step over the frame. You are in the meadow. The grass is soft, the sun is warm, the wind smells of hay. You are outside. You are free. You walk along the path, laughing, towards the hills.

The hills come no closer. The sun does not move. The wind keeps blowing the same way, through the same grass. You turn round: behind you, a gilded frame, and on the other side an old painter watching you, looking sorry.
"I only know how to paint pictures," he says.
You thought you were out. Your adventure ends here.
The gallery is long, narrow and silent. A red carpet, worn down to the weft, covers the floor. Candles burn in sconces, here and there, and their light trembles on the walls.
The walls are covered in portraits.

Hundreds of portraits, in gilded frames, hung side by side, from floor to ceiling. Men, women, young, old, in armour, in gowns, in rags, in travelling clothes. They all have the same expression: determined, a little anxious, turned upwards. They are adventurers. All those who climbed before you.
Under each portrait, a small brass plate bears a name, a date, and a caption. Always the same one: "Went back to 1."
You walk past them, slowly. It seems to you that their eyes follow you. At the end of the gallery, a low door opens onto a last staircase.
The portrait nearest the way out is hanging crooked. As though someone had taken it down, then hastily put it back.
If you go on, turn to {}.
If you take down the crooked portrait, turn to {}.
The door creaks on its hinges, long and slow, as though it has not been used for centuries, and then it lets you through.

The hall is so vast that your lantern cannot find its walls. The floor is made of great black and white flagstones, like a chessboard for giants, and your footsteps echo all the way up to the ceiling, far above. Tapestries hang in the shadows; they all show the same thing, the tower, and on each one the tower is a little taller.

In the middle of the hall, on a stool far too small for him, a guard is asleep, his chin on his chest. He snores with great dedication. An iron key, as long as your forearm, hangs from his belt and swings with every snore.
Somewhere behind him, someone is making soup. The smell comes in gusts: leeks, bacon, and something spicier that you cannot place.
If you tiptoe past him, turn to {}.
If you take the key, turn to {}.
If you politely wake the guard, turn to {}.
If you follow the smell of soup, turn to {}.
The handle turns without a sound. You bend down and go in.
There are brooms, then, a dozen of them, and buckets, and a mop drying on a nail. The door swings gently shut behind you, and on this side it has no handle.

You knock. You call out. Nobody comes. You wait a day, then two. To pass the time, you arrange the brooms by size, then by colour, then by wear. You learn to recognise the footsteps of the mice in the wall. You give each bucket a name.
Over the years, you get used to it. It is small, but it is clean, and it is home. Sometimes you hear someone pass on the staircase, on the other side of the door. You no longer knock.
You leave the guard to his snoring and follow your nose. The smell leads you through a service door, along a corridor with walls greasy with smoke, and into an enormous kitchen.

Everything in it is too big. The knives hanging on the wall are as long as swords. The saucepans could be used as bathtubs. On the fire, a cast-iron cauldron steams and bubbles, wide enough to bathe in, and the ladle lying across it is taller than you.
There is nobody here. On the table, a chopping board, half-chopped leeks, an apron thrown down in a heap. The cook has just stepped out. She will not be long.
At the back of the room there is the door of a larder. Against the wall, a kind of open cupboard hanging from a rope: a dumbwaiter, which disappears up a shaft towards the floors above.
If you taste the soup, turn to {}.
If you open the larder, turn to {}.
If you climb into the dumbwaiter, turn to {}.
You knock three times. The sound is that of real wood, hollow and resonant, which is not possible.
"Come in, it's open!" says a voice.

The painted door swings towards you, all by itself, with a little painted creak. Behind it there is a studio, full of light. Canvases everywhere, standing, lying down, stacked up, pots of paint, rags, brushes in jars. A large window looking out onto a perfect sky.
In the middle, in front of an easel, an old painter in a stained smock looks at you over his spectacles. He has paint in his beard, and a brush behind each ear.
"Ah, a visitor," he says. "Rare. Sit down."

He explains, while painting, that he has worked here for ever. That he paints the tower. That every floor he paints appears, somewhere, above the others. That the staircases, the rooms, the windows, they are all him. He looks tired, and rather proud.
If you ask him what is at the top, turn to {}.
If you ask him to paint you a way out, turn to {}.

The sound surrounds you before you even see where it comes from. Tick. Tock. So loud, so deep, that it no longer passes through your ears: it passes through your bones, your teeth, the floor under your soles.

You come out into a room as high as a cathedral, and it is full of gears. Cogwheels of every size, of copper, of iron, of blackened wood, turn into one another from floor to ceiling. The smallest are the size of plates and spin at full speed, whistling. The largest are as wide as houses and turn so slowly that it takes a moment to notice they are moving.
Huge pendulums swing above your head, from one wall to the other, blowing a warm wind. It smells of oil and hot metal.
All at once, you understand. The tower is not just a tower. It is a clock. And you are inside it.
In a corner, behind a dusty pane of glass, there is a small workshop, with a workbench, tools, and a seated figure that does not move.
If you climb up into the gears, turn to {}.
If you go and look at the workshop, turn to {}.
You are in a hurry. Everyone in this tower seems to have all the time in the world, except you. You take a run-up and jump onto the small wheel.
You catch it. It carries you off at once, at breakneck speed, towards the ray of daylight. You laugh. You are going to make it.

Then you reach the top of the wheel, and it keeps turning. Of course it does. That is what wheels do. It goes down the other side as fast as it came up, and takes you with it, down towards the other wheels, towards the teeth that mesh together and let through only what is very, very flat.
You should have thought of that. The small wheel turns faster than the big one. It is the only thing it knows how to do.
Somewhere in the room, a tick misses its tock. Just one. Then the clock picks up its rhythm again, as if nothing had happened.
You have always wanted to know how things are made inside. You take a screwdriver from the workbench, open the velvet waistcoat, then the panel of varnished wood, and you begin.

It is fascinating. There are hundreds of parts, thousands. You take them out one by one and lay them carefully on the workbench, in order, so that you can put everything back afterwards. Springs, cams, cylinders, a little copper heart that is still turning slightly.
When you have finished, there is no automaton any more. There is a workbench covered in parts, and a porcelain head looking at you.
You start putting it back together. You cannot do it. There are always parts left over.
Then the porcelain head begins to speak. "Don't worry," it says. "I know how to put things back together." And the parts start moving all by themselves, towards you.
They say that the automaton of the clock is bigger than before, and that he now has two eyes of different colours.
You greet the gardener, and he puts down his shears with pleasure, like someone who does not often get the chance to chat.
"Going up?" he says. "They all go up. Not many come through my garden, mind you. Most of them get lost before."
He offers you an apple, which you politely decline, given what you know about the fruit around here. He laughs. "Those ones are normal. It's the ones on the silver tree you mustn't touch."
You ask him the way. He shows you a stone staircase at the back of the terrace, which you had not seen behind the roses.
"That way is the sphinx," he says. "She guards the passage. She asks a question. Always the same one, I believe, but I've never heard it: I don't go up, myself, I have my roses."
He picks up his shears again, then adds, without looking at you: "A word of advice. When she asks you, never answer too quickly. People who answer too quickly, she likes them very much. For dinner."
Take the sphinx's staircase, and turn to {}.

The staircase climbs straight up, without a single bend, very steep. At times you climb on all fours, gripping the step above. The light of your lantern does not reach far: ahead, steps; behind, steps; on either side, stone.

After a long while, a step is missing. In its place there is a black hole, wide enough to make you hesitate, not wide enough to make you turn back. On the other side, the staircase carries on as though nothing had happened.

On your left, just before the hole, a corridor runs into the wall. A steady sound comes out of it, tick, tock, tick, tock, so loud it makes the stone tremble under your fingers. It sounds like the heart of the tower.
From the hole, you feel a cold breath rising. It makes you want to look.
If you jump over the hole, turn to {}.
If you look down, turn to {}.
If you take the corridor, turn to {}.
You do not know why you said that. It just came out. Perhaps because your grandmother used to repeat it all the time, that bread always goes up and never comes down.
The sphinx looks at you. For a long moment. Then her lips tremble. Her shoulders shake. And the sphinx bursts out laughing.

It is an immense laugh, enormous, a laugh that has not been used for centuries and comes out all at once, with all its strength. She rolls on the steps, paws in the air, she cries with laughter, she hiccups. The columns tremble. The staircase trembles. The whole tower trembles, from the cellar to the clouds, and somewhere below, a bell starts ringing all by itself.
You try to hold on to something. There is nothing to hold on to. The steps give way beneath your feet.
The sphinx goes on laughing long after your fall. They say that on certain evenings, you can still hear her.
You swing your leg over the window ledge and slide inside, onto a cold marble floor. The wind stops all at once, like a door closing.

You are in a small antechamber, its walls hung with velvet. In front of you, an archway opens onto a room from which comes the light you saw from outside. It dances on the walls, on the ceiling, on your hands: thousands of reflections, which move when you move.
You also hear footsteps. Footsteps very much like yours. When you stop, they stop.
On a little table there is a feather duster, a cloth, and a half-empty bottle of glass cleaner. Someone does the cleaning here, regularly. Someone is very keen for everything to shine.
Go into the room, and turn to {}.
You climb the rolling ladder. The rungs have been polished by generations of hands. You climb fast, higher and higher, the books sliding past your face, up to the top shelves, in the shadows.
There, you lean out to see whether there is a passage. You stretch out your arm. The ladder, beneath you, moves a little.

It rolls along its copper rail, gently at first, then faster, then very fast, with a metallic song, and you roll with it, clinging to the top, legs dangling in the void. The shelves rush past, one room, two rooms, ten rooms. The rail turns, the ladder turns, you turn.
At the end of the rail there is a wooden buffer, and the ladder stops dead against it.
The ladder stops. You do not.
You have been shelved ever since, somewhere in the library, between two bound volumes. The librarian has given you a shelf mark.
"A staircase," you say, rather pleased with yourself. It is a tower, after all. Stairs are all you have been doing since this morning.
The sphinx tilts her head. She looks almost disappointed.
"A staircase," she says softly, "goes down too. Ask all those who have fallen."

You open your mouth to explain that you meant a staircase where one only goes up, a special staircase, a staircase of the tower. But she has already risen. Standing, she is even bigger. She stretches her front paws, long and slow, like a cat waking from a nap.
"You answered too quickly," she says. "And I have been hungry for a very long time."

It is a narrow spiral staircase, where your shoulders brush both walls at once. It smells of wax and warm dust. The steps turn, always to the right, and after a hundred turns you are no longer quite sure where the hall was.
Candles burn in little niches, at regular intervals. They are new. You cannot see who could have lit them.

Halfway up, in the wall, there is a small low door. It is painted green, with a well-polished brass handle, and it is exactly your size, neither bigger nor smaller, as though someone had made it for you. Behind it, you hear nothing.
Above, the staircase keeps turning, and from very far away comes a glimmer, like a moving reflection.
If you keep climbing, turn to {}.
If you open the small door, turn to {}.

You take a step towards him. He takes a step towards you, with that slight delay, like someone hesitating. You turn left; he turns left. You walk on between the mirrors, and he guides you, without seeming to, from one glass to the next, always staying a little ahead of you.
The other reflections draw aside as he passes. They grow paler, blurrier, like a crowd breaking up at the end of a party. Soon only one is left: him.
He stops, in a large mirror with a gilded frame. You stop in front of it. You are nose to nose.

He looks exactly like you. The same eyes, the same coat, the same lantern, the same smudge of soot on the cheek. But when you raise your right hand, it is his right hand that rises too. Not the left, as an honest reflection would have it.
If you speak to him, turn to {}.
If you go on your way, turn to {}.
You climb down for a long time, hand over hand, feet against the wall. The circle of sky above you becomes a coin, then a dot, then nothing. At last your feet touch a floor of beaten earth.

You are under the tower. You can feel it in the weight of the silence, and in the air, which tastes of buried things. Your lantern lights up a round chamber with walls of raw rock, from which three tunnels lead away. Someone has dug steps here, ramps, passages: a great deal of work was done here, a very long time ago, to get somewhere.
On the wall above the tunnels, a sentence has been carved in clumsy letters: "Here, you go down to go up."

The tunnel on the left smells of water, a fresh, almost pleasant smell. In the middle one, a draught is blowing, making the flame of your lantern dance. The one on the right is the darkest. Your light does not go in. It stops at the edge, like a dog refusing to go any further.
If you take the tunnel that smells of water, turn to {}.
If you take the one where the air blows, turn to {}.
If you take the darkest one, turn to {}.

You pass beside the sphinx, so close that her fur brushes your arm. It is soft and warm. The sphinx does not move. She has already closed her eyes again, and her tail has started beating slowly on the marble once more.

The yellow marble staircase climbs on, between its columns. It is less hot now, and the smell of wild beast fades. The air grows lighter, colder, thinner, like mountain air. You feel very high up, higher than you have ever been, higher than the clouds perhaps.
At the top of the steps a gallery opens, long and dark, lit by a few candles. On its walls you can make out frames. A great many frames.
You turn round. The sphinx, below, has opened one eye. Just one. She is watching you.
If you go up to the gallery, turn to {}.
If you go back down a few steps to ask her one last piece of advice, turn to {}.
The boat slows down and comes to rest against the rock wall, of its own accord, like a dog against its master's leg.
In front of you, the rock is smooth, and someone has carved something into it. Not with a stonemason's chisel: with a knife, most likely, over many hours. The strokes are deep and careful.
It is a number, very large, in the middle of the wall:
And underneath, smaller, in a slightly shaky hand:
"One of the three. The other two are higher up. Do not forget it: up there, nobody will tell you again."
There is no signature. Only, in the corner, a little tower drawn in three strokes.

Beside the inscription, an iron ladder is set into the rock. It climbs towards a green glow, and a smell of leaves drifts down to you. Behind you, the river goes on its way, towards a golden brightness further on, which looks very much like daylight.
If you climb the ladder, turn to {}.
If you stay in the boat, turn to {}.

You push open the glass door of the workshop. A little bell tinkles. The room is tiny and cluttered: boxes of screws, springs, loose cogs, magnifying glasses, tweezers, dismantled clocks on every shelf.

The figure sitting at the workbench is an automaton. A man of metal and varnished wood, in a velvet waistcoat, with a porcelain head and two blue glass eyes. He holds fine tweezers in one hand and a tiny cog in the other, and he has stopped there, in the middle of a gesture, for who knows how long. Dust has settled on his shoulders like snow.
In his back, between the shoulder blades, there is a large brass key, like those on clockwork toys.
On the workbench, a label reads, in a neat hand: "Clockmaker. To be wound once a century." The date of the last time has been worn away by time.
If you wind him up, turn to {}.
If you take him apart to see how he is made, turn to {}.

You put your hand against the glass. It is not cold. It is warm, and it gives, like the surface of water. Your fingers pass through. His pass the other way. You feel a shiver, a dizziness, the world flipping over like a pancake.
You are on the other side.

Everything is the same, but back to front. The letters on your belt read from right to left. Your heart beats on the wrong side. And before you, in the room, standing on the real floor, there is you. He flexes his fingers, he breathes deeply, he looks around him with immense happiness.
Then he picks up the lantern, your lantern, and walks off towards the stairs, without looking back.
You wait for him. You wait for a long time. Sometimes a traveller passes through the room, and you do everything he does, just a little late.
You do not have the numbers. Or you do not have the patience. You have climbed so many stairs, faced so many things, that a little door of pale wood is not going to stop you.
You take three steps back and hurl yourself at it, shoulder first.

The door saw that coming. It does not move, but the landing does. The flagstones tip under your feet like the boards of a trapdoor, and you discover that under this bare landing there was a very long shaft, very straight, very dark, running all the way down. All the way to the first well, perhaps. The one with the new rope.
On the way down, you have time to pass every floor you climbed. It is not a pleasant sight, at that speed.
Here you are before the face of the clock, on the narrow stone ledge, in the wind. The Roman numerals are taller than you. The black iron hands point upwards.

You look at the time. It is one minute to noon. You wait. It is still one minute to noon. The minute hand trembles, as if it wanted to move, but it does not move. You understand that it has been one minute to noon for a very long time, and will be for a very long time to come. It is the tower's hour. It has no other.
At the foot of the clock face, almost hidden by the numeral VI, there is a small iron trapdoor with a ring. It leads back inside the tower, upwards.

Above your head hangs a bronze bell, enormous, green with age. A rope runs down from its clapper to within reach of your hand. You badly want to pull it, just to see. To announce to the whole tower that you are here.
If you go through the trapdoor, turn to {}.
If you ring the bell, turn to {}.

The minute hand is almost vertical. It climbs up the clock face like a ladder, and its tip is lost above you, higher than the ledge, higher than anything you could reach any other way. It is an opportunity.
You grab hold of it, with both hands, with both legs, and start climbing the cold iron.
The hand moves. Clack. One minute. You are a little higher. Clack. Another. You keep climbing. It is almost noon. Three minutes to go. Two. One.

All the bells of the tower ring at once, and the hand, having reached the top of the face, does what all hands do at noon: it carries on. It passes noon. It starts to lean the other way, slowly, then decidedly.
At the far end of the hall of mirrors, where the reflections finally run out, there are two doors.

They are identical. The same dark wood, the same nails, the same knocker shaped like a hand, the same scratch on the bottom panel. It looks as if one were the reflection of the other, except that no mirror stands between them.

You look at them for a long time, head tilted. Then you notice the difference. On the right-hand door, the knocker is held by a left hand. And the little brass plate bearing the door's number is written backwards, as if read in a mirror.

From behind the left-hand door comes a rising draught, and a faint sound, like footsteps going round and round. From behind the right-hand one, the backwards one, comes a smell of cut grass and damp earth. A bird is singing. Backwards, perhaps, but it is singing.
If you open the left-hand door, turn to {}.
If you open the backwards door, turn to {}.
You raise the ladle above your head, like a knight with his sword. It is heavy, it drips with soup, but you stand firm.

The ogress turns round. She looks at you, and at your ladle. She says nothing. She wipes her hands on her apron, calmly. Then she reaches towards the wall, where her utensils hang, and takes down her own.
You do not have time to apologise. The last sound you hear is very much like a gong.

You fold yourself in two, then in four, and squeeze into the dumbwaiter, between a pile of dirty plates and a basket of stale bread. Your knees touch your chin. This was not made for a traveller, it was made for a roast.

In front of your nose, a thick rope runs from top to bottom. It disappears upwards into a black shaft that smells of grease and smoke, and downwards into a creaking pulley. By pulling on it, you ought to be able to go up.
You put your hands on the rope. It is rough, a little sticky. It vibrates faintly, as if, very far up, someone else were holding it too.
If you pull hard, turn to {}.
If you pull gently, turn to {}.
If you cut the rope, turn to {}.
You lift the crooked portrait, to straighten it, or to see what it hides. It is light. Behind it, on the wall, there is another frame.
An empty frame. Gilded, like the others. With, beneath it, a small brass plate, brand new and shining. It bears your name. A date: today. And a caption you already know.

You step back. The empty frame comes closer. Or perhaps it is you. You no longer know. It is just your size, and it is very beautiful, and it seems to have been waiting for you for ever, like the little green door on the staircase, like the blue boat on the river.
It suits you very well. Everyone who passes through the gallery, ever since, stops in front of your portrait. They think you look determined, a little anxious, turned upwards.
The tunnel slopes gently down, and the smell of water grows stronger, and then a sound answers it: a lapping, a murmur, the song of a river you cannot see yet.

It appears all at once, round a bend in the rock. An underground river, black and smooth, as wide as a street. It flows unhurriedly under a vault where points of light are shining, little stones that sparkle like stars. It looks like an upside-down sky.

After seven years, the bad luck goes away. So do you, but not in the right direction.
A key like that must open something, up there. You creep closer, one hand outstretched, holding your breath. The guard is still snoring. Your fingers close on the cold iron. You pull, ever so gently.

He had only been sleeping with one eye, and unfortunately it was the other one. He looks at you for a long moment, without anger, with a kind of weariness, like someone who has seen a hundred thieves before you and will see a hundred more. Then he stands up.
Sitting down, he was tall. Standing up, he is much taller. His head disappears somewhere in the shadows of the hall, and you understand, too late, why his stool looked so small.
"The key," he says, in a voice that makes the flagstones tremble, "opens nothing. It is me it guards."
You run to the balloon, jump into the basket, and undo the knot in the rope. The gardener shouts something behind you. You do not hear it: the balloon is already rising.

It passes through the shaft, and there you are, outside, in the sky. The wind carries you away, soft and warm. The tower slides past beside you, window after window. Then the clouds, which you pass through in a white shiver. Then the blue sky, immense, above everything.
You are higher than the tower. You have won. You laugh, you shout, you wave your arms.

Then you look beside you. The tower is still there. It goes on, above the clouds, long after the clouds, and it keeps rising, beside your balloon, as high as you, higher than you. It has no end, even here.
And your balloon, rising less and less, begins to hiss softly. The gas is running out.
You thought you had won. Your adventure ends here.

The well stands at the foot of the wall, where the tower comes out of the ground. Its rim is made of stones older than those of the tower, polished by hands that have leaned on them for centuries. It is warm, as if something were breathing underneath.
You lean over. There is no water. There is no smell of mud, no frogs, no bucket. There is only a perfect circle of black, and a rope, tied to an iron ring, going down into it and vanishing.
The rope is new. It is the only new thing here. Someone tied it with care, with a sailor's knot, and left it there. For you, perhaps. Or for someone else, who never pulled it back up.
A round pebble lies on the rim, within easy reach.
If you climb down the rope, turn to {}.
If you drop the pebble first, to see, turn to {}.

You keep climbing. The ivy grows thinner, its stems finer, sparser, and your hands have to search for every hold. The wind is blowing hard now. The clouds are very close. You pass through one, cold and wet, which leaves your eyelashes full of drops.
And then the ivy stops. Just like that. Above you the tower goes on, but the stone is smooth, without a crack, without a hold. Even a fly would slide off it.
Just above your head, in the last fork of the ivy, there is a nest. A very large nest, made of branches, rags, bent spoons and all kinds of shiny things. Something in it is glowing softly.
A little further down, on your right, another window is open. This one looks out onto green: leaves, flowers, a garden, at this height.
If you look into the nest, turn to {}.
If you climb back down to the garden window, turn to {}.

You climb. The steps turn, and turn, always to the left, around the white pillar. The fresco slides past on the wall: hills, a windmill, a river, a shepherd, sheep, a path, a hedge, birds, a sky clouding over.
You climb on. Your legs begin to ache.

That cracked step, you have seen it before. That shepherd too, with his crooked hat. That windmill. That stain on the wall, shaped like a rabbit. You have been here before. You are sure of it. Or else it is another cracked step, another shepherd, another stain, and the staircase repeats itself, like a song coming back to the chorus.
You stop to catch your breath. Below, the spiral. Above, the spiral. On the wall, the fresco, which seems to watch you climbing, patiently.
If you keep climbing, turn to {}.
If you notice the little painted door on the wall, turn to {}.
If you go back down, turn to {}.

The ladder below the trapdoor is old, and its rungs groan under your weight. Down below, the cellar is low and vaulted, full of barrels lying side by side. Some of them bear dates. The oldest are so old that you cannot read them.
Cobwebs hang between the vaults, grey and thick. Nobody has lived in them for a long time.

You walk between the barrels. At the far end of the cellar, the wall has collapsed: a heap of stones, earth and roots, and behind it a black hole breathing out damp air. A tunnel. It goes down into the earth, under the tower, on a gentle slope.
You hesitate. You came here to go up, not down. But you remember what your grandmother used to say, and she had travelled a great deal: sometimes you have to go down to go up.
You pick up the pebble, hold your arm out over the hole and let it go. Then you count, the way you were taught, to find out how deep it is.
One. Two. Three. You listen. Four. Five. Six.

You count to twenty. Then to a hundred, feeling a little foolish, leaning over a well, counting to yourself in the wind. You never hear it hit the bottom. No knock on stone, no splash, not the slightest echo. The pebble is gone, that is all, and the well has kept it.
You look at the rope. It still goes down into the dark, pulled tight, quite unconcerned by your sums. It, at least, seems to know where it is going.
If you climb down anyway, turn to {}.
If you give up on the well and retrace your steps, turn to {}.

You close your eyes. No more reflections, no more crowd, no more dizziness: only the darkness behind your eyelids, and the sound of your footsteps. You hold your hands out in front of you and walk straight, as straight as you can.

One step, two steps, ten steps. You bang your forehead against a mirror, hard enough to see stars that have nothing to do with the ones in the sky. You swear. A thousand of you swear at the same time, no doubt, but you cannot see them, and that is a relief.
You feel your way along the mirror. It is smooth, endless. Then your fingers meet something else: wood. A frame. And in the middle of the frame, a cold metal handle, shaped like a cogwheel.
Behind the door, you hear a steady, powerful sound that makes the wood vibrate under your hand. Tick. Tock. Tick. Tock.
Open the door, and turn to {}.
You come out into a garden.

It cannot possibly be there, at this height, inside a tower of stone, and yet there it is. A terraced garden, rising over several levels, with paths of white gravel, beds of flowers whose names you do not know, ponds where goldfish swim. The light falls from a shaft open to the sky, very high up, green and golden through the leaves.

Birds are singing. Bees go by, laden with pollen. The air is soft, it smells of damp earth, of roses and mint. After so much stone and darkness, you want to lie down in the grass and never set off again.

In the middle of the first terrace, a marble fountain murmurs. Beside it grows a tree with silver leaves, laden with round fruit the colour of a sunset, glowing softly. Further on, a path crosses the garden towards the upper terraces.
If you drink from the fountain, turn to {}.
If you pick a fruit and eat it, turn to {}.
If you cross the garden, turn to {}.
You walk into a room where there is no one but you.

You, everywhere. The walls are covered in mirrors, from floor to ceiling, and the ceiling too, and even the floor, polished like frozen water. Each mirror sends you back into another mirror, which sends you into another, and so on, for ever. You are a thousand. You are ten thousand. A crowd of yourselves, in close ranks, stretching away in every direction and raising the lantern at the same time as you.
You take a step. The crowd takes a step. You no longer know where the walls are, nor which way you came in. There are corridors that are not corridors, doors that are only reflections of doors.
In the crowd, though, one of you is not doing quite the same as the others. He is a little late. And he is looking, not straight ahead, but at you.
If you follow that reflection, turn to {}.
If you close your eyes and walk straight ahead, turn to {}.
If you break a mirror to clear a way through, turn to {}.
An idea comes to you, brilliant, like all bad ideas: if the dumbwaiter goes up when you pull the rope, it will surely go up much faster if you cut it. It is physics. More or less.
You take out your knife. The rope is tough, and you have to saw for a long time. At last, the final strand gives way.
The dumbwaiter immediately starts going much faster. You were right about that. You were only wrong about the direction.
The dirty plates go up. You go down, very fast, into the dark, with the basket of stale bread and a thought for physics.
You accept. The crows spread out around you, each one takes hold of a bit of sleeve, of collar, of belt, of bootlace. "On three," says the big crow. On two, they take off.
It is marvellous. The tower rushes past, the windows, the floors, the ivy shrinking below. The clouds draw near. You laugh, they caw, the wind carries you.

Then a crow at your left sleeve says that you ought to go round by the east. Another, at your collar, says that the east is nonsense. A third asks what the east is. The big crow calls for silence. Nobody listens to him.
The argument grows heated. Everyone wants to be right. To make their point more clearly, each of them lets go of what they were holding, to flap their wings.
They are still arguing, very high up, when you reach the bottom.

You cross the library looking for a way out. The hexagonal rooms follow one after another, all alike, and you soon understand that you must not wander far: you could walk in here all your life without ever seeing the same shelf twice.
Fortunately, in the first room there are three ways to leave.
In one corner, a stone staircase climbs, narrow and steep. A strange smell comes down it, a smell of wild beast, warm sand and incense. Very high up, you can hear something like slow breathing.

Against a bookcase, a tall rolling ladder stands on its copper rail. It climbs to the highest shelves, right up there, where it is so dark you cannot see the ceiling. There may be a passage up there. There is always a passage at the top of a library.
And on the far wall, between two bookcases, a window stands ajar. A smell of flowers comes in through the gap, and a ray of green light, like the light that passes through leaves.
If you take the staircase, turn to {}.
If you climb the rolling ladder, turn to {}.
If you go through the window, turn to {}.
You climb the last steps, and you come out onto a landing of bare stone.

There is nothing here. No window, no candle, no carpet, no portrait. Only the stone, grey and cold, and a pale light coming from who knows where. The silence is total. You no longer hear the clock, nor the wind, nor the birds. You are above all that.
In front of you, there is a door.

It is plain, of pale wood, without ornament. It has no handle. It has no keyhole. Instead, there is a brass plate with three small dials, and on each dial, numbers. Above the dials, engraved in the brass, an inscription:
"Three numbers were given to you on your way up, by three who do not lie. Add them together. The total will open the door."
If you know the three numbers, add them together, and turn to the paragraph with that number.
If you do not know them, or if you would rather find another way in:
If you force the door, turn to {}.
If you knock on the door, turn to {}.
You were always taught to be polite. When someone waves at you, you wave back. It is the least you can do, and you are glad to see someone at last, after so much solitude.
You raise your hand to answer.
Only then do you notice a detail. To wave, you have to let go of the ivy. And to hold on to the ivy, halfway up an endless tower, in a wind tugging at your clothes, you need two hands. Not one. Two.

You have plenty of time to think about it on the way down. You also have time to see the figure below grow, and grow, and to understand that it was not someone waving: it was a scarecrow, whose arm was moving in the wind.
You follow the gravel path, from terrace to terrace. The garden climbs with you, and grows wilder as it goes: the flowerbeds tangle together, roses climb the walls, the grass comes up to your knees.

On the highest terrace, a gardener is at work. He is a small round man in a straw hat, clipping a hedge with large shears, whistling. The hedge is immense, and he has given it a strange shape: that of a staircase. A staircase of box, with neat steps, climbing along the wall and vanishing into the foliage, right at the top.

Further on, at the edge of the terrace, tied to a post by a rope, a hot-air balloon sways gently. Its envelope is striped red and yellow, its basket made of wicker, and it tugs at its rope like an impatient dog. Above it, the shaft opens onto the sky.
The gardener has seen you. He raises his hat politely, without stopping his clipping.
If you speak to the gardener, turn to {}.
If you climb the hedge shaped like a staircase, turn to {}.
If you get into the hot-air balloon, turn to {}.
One, two, three. You count under your breath, touching the rail at every step. It is an old habit: counting is knowing where you are, and knowing where you are is a little like not being lost.
Four, five, six. The fresco slides past on your left, hills, a windmill, a river. Ten. Eleven. Twelve. A shepherd with his sheep, a sky slowly clouding over.

The seventeenth step is not like the others. Someone has carved an arrow into it, a simple little arrow, with the tip of a knife, and it does not point to the top of the stairs. It points to the wall.

You look at the wall. There is the fresco, still: a path, a hedge, and in the hedge a small wooden door, rounded at the top, with a black handle. It is so well painted that you would take it for a real one.
If you follow the arrow to the door, turn to {}.
If you stop counting and climb, turn to {}.
You reach for the handle, grasp it firmly, and pull.
Your fingers close on plaster. You had seen it, though: it is a painting. But you were so sure of yourself, and it was so well done, that you took a run-up to go through as you opened it.

The impact is dull. The wall does not move. You do. A little. You find yourself flattened against the fresco, between the hedge and the path, arms spread wide, and the paint, still fresh at this spot, sticks to you all over.

When the next travellers come up the staircase, they stop to admire this detail of the painting: a figure flattened against a door, looking very surprised. They think it is the best part of the whole fresco.

The ivy covers a whole side of the tower, from the ground up to heights where it is no more than a green shadow. Its stems are as thick as arms, twisted, intertwined, and its leaves so many that you can no longer see the stone behind them.

You put your hand on it. It is alive, it is solid, it is warm from the sun. Deep in the foliage something rustles, small creatures moving out of your way. Very high up, black birds circle the tower, crying out.
You have always been a good climber. Trees, garden walls, forbidden attics. But you have never climbed this high, and you have never climbed something that has no top.
One stem hangs in front of you, thicker than the others, like a rope held out to you. It looks solid. It looks it, anyway.
If you start climbing, turn to {}.
If you first pull on the stem with all your strength, to test it, turn to {}.
You run. Your feet slap on the flagstones, the lantern bangs against your leg, and behind you the guard lets out an enormous growl, like a bear disturbed in its winter sleep.

You wait for the sound of him running after you. It does not come. You glance over your shoulder: the guard has simply turned over on his stool, propped his cheek on his hand, and gone back to sleep. Nobody, it seems, has ever paid him to run.

You catch your breath at the foot of a staircase. It goes straight up, without a landing, without a rail, so steep it looks like a ladder carved into the stone. The steps are hollowed in the middle, worn by the feet that climbed before you. A great many feet. You wonder how many came back down.

You climb the first steps, slowly, your hands in plain sight. The sphinx lets you approach. When you are so close that you can feel her breath, warm and perfumed, she speaks. Her voice is deep, and gentle, and it echoes inside you more than outside.
"Traveller. All who go up pass by me. All who pass by me answer. All who answer wrongly stay."
She smiles. Her teeth are white and pointed.
"Listen carefully. What always goes up, and never comes down?"
Silence falls on the staircase. The sphinx's tail has stopped beating. Her cat's eyes do not leave you.

You think of the tower, of course. You think of the stairs you have climbed since morning. You think of something else too, something simpler, which rises in each of us, gently, without ever going back.
If you answer "a staircase", turn to {}.
If you answer "the price of bread", turn to {}.
You pick up the little book. Its cover is black, with a green band across the top. The title is written in gold letters: *The Book with No Ending*. And underneath, by hand: *… except one?*
You open it at random. It is made of numbered paragraphs. You land on number ninety-eight, and you read:
"You pick up the little book. Its cover is black, with a green band across the top. The title is written in gold letters…"

You stop. You read it again. It is exactly what is happening to you. The book tells what you are doing, at the very moment you are doing it. You read on with a shiver: the book says that you stop, that you read it again, that you shiver.
Then the paragraph ends, like all the others, with a line in bold:
If you do as the book says, turn to {}.
If you close the book, very quickly, turn to {}.
You keep reading. One page, then another. The word must come back somewhere. And if there is one, perhaps there are two. A sentence. A whole book that makes sense, hidden in this gibberish.

You sit down on the floor, your back against the shelf. You read. You finish the book. You take another. You read on. The light never changes in the library: there is no day and no night, no hunger and no tiredness, only the next page.
You read on. You will read for ever. Sometimes you think you have found a word, and your heart beats faster, and you turn the page.
You no longer think about the tower. You no longer think about the top. You no longer quite know why you came.
Turn back to {}, if you can.
It opens without effort, and you climb out, and there are no more steps.

There are no more walls. There is no more ceiling. There is the sky, everywhere, above you, around you, and even a little below you, between the clouds. An immense sky, blue, deep, washed clean, crossed by a wind that has never touched a stone.
You are at the top. It is a small round platform, hardly bigger than a table, and there is nothing on it. No treasure. No throne. No answer written down. Just you, and the wind, and all this light.
You think of the old painter, down below, who did not know what was missing to finish his tower. You know now. What was missing was someone who reached the top.
You think of the ogress. You will tell her that it was good right to the end.
You stay there for a long time, looking at the sky. Perhaps you will never go back down. It does not matter. You have arrived.
